# Problem 1: Logistic Regression for Homicide Resolution

## Data Import and Cleaning
```{r p1-01-import-data}
homicide_raw =
  read_csv(
    "data/homicide-data.csv",
    na = c("", "NA", "Unknown")
  )
```

```{r p1-02-clean-data}
homicide_df =
  homicide_raw |>
  mutate(
    city_state = str_c(city, state, sep = ", "),
    resolved = as.numeric(disposition == "Closed by arrest"),
    victim_age = as.numeric(victim_age)
  ) |>
  filter(
    !city_state %in% c(
      "Dallas, TX",
      "Phoenix, AZ",
      "Kansas City, MO",
      "Tulsa, AL"
    ),
    victim_race %in% c("White", "Black"),
    victim_sex %in% c("Female", "Male")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    victim_race = fct_relevel(victim_race, "White"),
    victim_sex = fct_relevel(victim_sex, "Female")
  ) |>
  select(
    city_state, resolved, victim_age,
    victim_race, victim_sex
  ) |>
  drop_na()
```


```{r p1-03-check-data}
homicide_df |>
  summarize(
    n_observations = n(),
    n_cities = n_distinct(city_state),
    n_missing_age = sum(is.na(victim_age))
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()

homicide_df |>
  count(victim_race, victim_sex) |>
  knitr::kable()

homicide_df |>
  count(resolved) |>
  mutate(proportion = n / sum(n)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The homicide data were obtained from The Washington Post's public GitHub repository. 
I created a city-state identifier and a binary outcome indicating whether a homicide 
was resolved by arrest. Dallas, TX; Phoenix, AZ; Kansas City, MO; and Tulsa, 
AL were excluded as specified in the assignment. The analysis was restricted to 
Black and White victims with known sex and complete model covariates. 
Victim age was converted to a numeric variable, and female and White victims 
were selected as the reference categories.

After data cleaning, the final analytical dataset consisted of 39,362 homicide records 
across 47 cities, with no missing values for victim age. Of these cases, 
19,207 (48.8%) were resolved by arrest, while 20,155 (51.2%) were not. 
The majority of records involved Black male victims, accounting for 73.9% of the analytical sample.



## Logistic Regression for Baltimore
```{r p1-04-baltimore-model}
baltimore_df =
  homicide_df |>
  filter(city_state == "Baltimore, MD")

baltimore_fit =
  baltimore_df |>
  glm(
    resolved ~ victim_age + victim_sex + victim_race,
    data = _,
    family = binomial()
  )
```

```{r p1-05-baltimore-or}
baltimore_or =
  baltimore_fit |>
  broom::tidy(
    conf.int = TRUE,
    exponentiate = TRUE
  ) |>
  filter(term == "victim_sexMale") |>
  select(
    term,
    OR = estimate,
    conf.low,
    conf.high
  )

baltimore_or |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c(
      "Predictor",
      "Adjusted OR",
      "95% CI Lower",
      "95% CI Upper"
    )
  )
```

I fitted a multivariable logistic regression model for Baltimore, MD, with homicide resolution 
as the outcome and victim age, sex, and race as predictors. After adjusting for victim age 
and race, homicides involving male victims had approximately 57.4% lower odds 
of being resolved by arrest than those involving female victims 
(adjusted OR = 0.426, 95% CI: 0.324–0.558). The confidence interval did not include 1, 
indicating a statistically significant association between victim sex and homicide resolution 
in Baltimore.



## Logistic Regression Across Cities
```{r p1-06-city-models}
city_models =
  homicide_df |>
  nest(datasets = -city_state) |>
  mutate(
    fits = map(
      datasets,
      \(df) glm(
        resolved ~ victim_age + victim_sex + victim_race,
        data = df,
        family = binomial()
      )
    ),
    results = map(
      fits,
      \(fit) broom::tidy(
        fit,
        conf.int = TRUE,
        exponentiate = TRUE
      )
    )
  )
```


```{r p1-07-city-or}
city_or_df =
  city_models |>
  select(city_state, results) |>
  unnest(results) |>
  filter(term == "victim_sexMale") |>
  select(
    city_state,
    OR = estimate,
    conf.low,
    conf.high
  ) |>
  arrange(OR)

city_or_df
```

I fitted separate logistic regression models for all 47 cities using nested data frames 
and the `map()` function. Each model included victim age, sex, and race as predictors, 
with female and White victims serving as the reference categories. The model coefficients 
and confidence limits were exponentiated to obtain city-specific adjusted odds ratios 
and 95% confidence intervals comparing male victims with female victims. The results were 
then combined into a single tidy data frame and ordered by the estimated odds ratios.

As a consistency check, the Baltimore estimate obtained from the city-specific analysis 
matched the result from the individual logistic regression model 
(adjusted OR = 0.426, 95% CI: 0.324–0.558), confirming that the iterative modeling 
workflow reproduced the Baltimore result.


## Comparison of City-Specific Odds Ratios
```{r p1-08-city-or-plot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 13}
city_or_df |>
  mutate(
    city_state = fct_reorder(city_state, OR)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = city_state, y = OR)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high),
    width = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 1,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "red"
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Adjusted Odds Ratios for Homicide Resolution by City",
    subtitle = "Male versus female victims, adjusted for age and race",
    x = "City",
    y = "Adjusted odds ratio (95% CI)"
  )

theme(
  axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9),
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
)
```

```{r p1-09-city-or-summary}
city_or_df |>
  summarize(
    n_cities = n(),
    n_or_below_one = sum(OR < 1),
    n_ci_below_one = sum(conf.high < 1),
    n_ci_above_one = sum(conf.low > 1),
    n_ci_includes_one = sum(
      conf.low <= 1 & conf.high >= 1
    )
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Across the 47 cities included in the analysis, 41 (87.2%) had adjusted odds ratios 
below 1, suggesting that homicides involving male victims generally had lower odds 
of being resolved by arrest than those involving female victims after adjustment 
for victim age and race.

The magnitude and precision of the estimated associations varied considerably 
across cities. The adjusted odds ratios ranged from 0.262 in New York, 
NY (95% CI: 0.133–0.485), to 1.767 in Albuquerque, NM (95% CI: 0.825–3.762). 
Of the 47 cities, 22 had 95% confidence intervals entirely below 1, 
while the remaining 25 had confidence intervals that included 1. 
No city had a confidence interval entirely above 1.

Overall, the results suggest a broadly consistent pattern of lower odds of 
homicide resolution for male victims, although the strength and statistical 
precision of this association varied across cities.
